claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 are novel paralogous C. elegans germ granule components that interact with the intrinsically disordered MEG-3 protein.
source: We describe MIP-1 and MIP-2, novel paralogous C. elegans germ granule components that interact with the intrinsically disordered MEG-3 protein.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 promote P granule condensation.
source: These proteins promote P granule condensation, form granules independently of MEG-3 in the postembryonic germ line, and balance each other in regulating P granule growth and localization.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 form granules independently of MEG-3 in the postembryonic germ line.
source: These proteins promote P granule condensation, form granules independently of MEG-3 in the postembryonic germ line, and balance each other in regulating P granule growth and localization.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 balance each other in regulating P granule growth and localization.
source: These proteins promote P granule condensation, form granules independently of MEG-3 in the postembryonic germ line, and balance each other in regulating P granule growth and localization.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 each contain two LOTUS domains and intrinsically disordered regions.
source: MIP-1 and MIP-2 each contain two LOTUS domains and intrinsically disordered regions and form homo- and heterodimers.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 form homo- and heterodimers.
source: MIP-1 and MIP-2 each contain two LOTUS domains and intrinsically disordered regions and form homo- and heterodimers.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 bind and anchor the Vasa homolog GLH-1 within P granules.
source: They bind and anchor the Vasa homolog GLH-1 within P granules and are jointly required for coalescence of MEG-3, GLH-1, and PGL proteins.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 are jointly required for coalescence of MEG-3, GLH-1, and PGL proteins.
source: They bind and anchor the Vasa homolog GLH-1 within P granules and are jointly required for coalescence of MEG-3, GLH-1, and PGL proteins.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: Animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 show temperature-sensitive embryonic lethality.
source: Animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 show temperature-sensitive embryonic lethality, sterility, and mortal germ lines.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: Animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 show sterility.
source: Animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 show temperature-sensitive embryonic lethality, sterility, and mortal germ lines.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: Animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 show mortal germ lines.
source: Animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 show temperature-sensitive embryonic lethality, sterility, and mortal germ lines.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: Germline phenotypes in animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 include defects in stem cell self-renewal.
source: Germline phenotypes include defects in stem cell self-renewal, meiotic progression, and gamete differentiation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: Germline phenotypes in animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 include defects in meiotic progression.
source: Germline phenotypes include defects in stem cell self-renewal, meiotic progression, and gamete differentiation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: Germline phenotypes in animals lacking MIP-1 and MIP-2 include defects in gamete differentiation.
source: Germline phenotypes include defects in stem cell self-renewal, meiotic progression, and gamete differentiation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: Germ granules are membraneless cytoplasmic compartments with liquid-like properties that form by liquid-liquid phase separation from the bulk cytoplasm.
source: A common feature of germ cells is the presence of germ granules, membraneless cytoplasmic compartments with liquid-like properties that form by liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) from the bulk cytoplasm (Brangwynne et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brangwynne et al., 2009.

claim: Germ granules are rich in both RNA and RNA-binding proteins.
source: Rich in both RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), germ granules contain a large number of molecules with roles in post-transcriptional RNA regulation and the preservation of genome integrity (Mayya and Duchaine, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayya and Duchaine, 2019.

claim: Germ granules contain a large number of molecules with roles in post-transcriptional RNA regulation and the preservation of genome integrity.
source: Rich in both RNA and RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), germ granules contain a large number of molecules with roles in post-transcriptional RNA regulation and the preservation of genome integrity (Mayya and Duchaine, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mayya and Duchaine, 2019.

claim: Germ granules are important for the specification, maintenance, and normal development of the germ line.
source: These complex ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assemblies are important for the specification, maintenance, and normal development of the germ line (Knutson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knutson et al., 2017.

claim: Polarization of the C. elegans embryo upon fertilization triggers differential anterior-posterior phosphorylation of multiple regulatory proteins.
source: Polarization of the embryo upon fertilization triggers differential anterior-posterior phosphorylation of multiple regulatory proteins, resulting in concentration gradients that provide a permissive environment for germ granule condensation only in the posterior (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Seydoux, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2009 and Seydoux, 2018.

claim: Differential anterior-posterior phosphorylation results in concentration gradients that provide a permissive environment for germ granule condensation only in the posterior of C. elegans embryos.
source: Polarization of the embryo upon fertilization triggers differential anterior-posterior phosphorylation of multiple regulatory proteins, resulting in concentration gradients that provide a permissive environment for germ granule condensation only in the posterior (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Seydoux, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2009 and Seydoux, 2018.

claim: C. elegans germ granules are called P granules because during embryogenesis they segregate uniquely to the posterior cell lineage.
source: C. elegans germ granules are called P granules because during embryogenesis they segregate uniquely to the posterior cell lineage (P0-P4 and Z2/Z3), those cells that will give rise to the future germ line (Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2010.

claim: P granules are cytoplasmic in very early C. elegans embryos.
source: P granules are cytoplasmic in very early embryos, begin to coalesce around the nuclear periphery at the four-cell stage, and thereafter form perinuclear foci in all germ cells (Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2010.

claim: P granules begin to coalesce around the nuclear periphery at the four-cell stage in C. elegans embryos.
source: P granules are cytoplasmic in very early embryos, begin to coalesce around the nuclear periphery at the four-cell stage, and thereafter form perinuclear foci in all germ cells (Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2010.

claim: P granules form perinuclear foci in all germ cells after the four-cell stage.
source: P granules are cytoplasmic in very early embryos, begin to coalesce around the nuclear periphery at the four-cell stage, and thereafter form perinuclear foci in all germ cells (Updike and Strome, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Updike and Strome, 2010.

claim: Nucleation of P granules in the zygote requires the intrinsically disordered, serine-rich protein MEG-3.
source: Nucleation of P granules in the zygote requires the intrinsically disordered, serine-rich protein MEG-3 (previously known as GEI-12) (Chen et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: A putative null allele of meg-3 is not sterile on its own.
source: A putative null allele of meg-3 is not sterile on its own, but does show sterility when combined with mutations in its paralog meg-4 (30%), meg-1 (40%), or both (100%) (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: A putative null allele of meg-3 shows sterility when combined with mutations in its paralog meg-4 (30%).
source: A putative null allele of meg-3 is not sterile on its own, but does show sterility when combined with mutations in its paralog meg-4 (30%), meg-1 (40%), or both (100%) (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: A putative null allele of meg-3 shows sterility when combined with mutations in meg-1 (40%).
source: A putative null allele of meg-3 is not sterile on its own, but does show sterility when combined with mutations in its paralog meg-4 (30%), meg-1 (40%), or both (100%) (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: A putative null allele of meg-3 shows 100% sterility when combined with mutations in both meg-4 and meg-1.
source: A putative null allele of meg-3 is not sterile on its own, but does show sterility when combined with mutations in its paralog meg-4 (30%), meg-1 (40%), or both (100%) (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: Transgenerational RNAi of meg-3 gives rise to progressive loss of fertility.
source: Transgenerational RNAi of meg-3 gives rise to progressive loss of fertility (Chen et al., 2016), presumably due to additional off-target knock-down of meg-4, which encodes a protein that is 71% identical to MEG-3 (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: MEG-4 encodes a protein that is 71% identical to MEG-3.
source: Transgenerational RNAi of meg-3 gives rise to progressive loss of fertility (Chen et al., 2016), presumably due to additional off-target knock-down of meg-4, which encodes a protein that is 71% identical to MEG-3 (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: MEG-3 binds RNA non-specifically and recruits numerous mRNAs into P granules.
source: MEG-3 binds RNA non-specifically and recruits numerous mRNAs into P granules (Lee et al., 2020), while a MEX-5 gradient suppresses granule formation in the anterior by competing with MEG-3 for binding to RNAs (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: A MEX-5 gradient suppresses granule formation in the anterior by competing with MEG-3 for binding to RNAs.
source: MEG-3 binds RNA non-specifically and recruits numerous mRNAs into P granules (Lee et al., 2020), while a MEX-5 gradient suppresses granule formation in the anterior by competing with MEG-3 for binding to RNAs (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2016.

claim: In vitro, MEG-3 forms gel-like condensates that are enhanced by the presence of RNA and antagonized by MEX-5.
source: In vitro, MEG-3 also forms gel-like condensates that are enhanced by the presence of RNA and antagonized by MEX-5 (Lee et al., 2020; Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2020 and Putnam et al., 2019.

claim: MEG-3 is part of a regulatory network that controls P granule formation in early embryos.
source: Thus, MEG-3 is part of a regulatory network that controls P granule formation in early embryos.
evidence: Inferred from the preceding discussion of MEG-3 functions.

claim: Phase separation of proteins with intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) is a hallmark of germ granules and other non-membranous organelles.
source: Phase separation of proteins with intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) is a hallmark of germ granules and other non-membranous organelles that carry out diverse core cellular processes, including gene transcription, ribosome biogenesis, cytoskeletal organization, stress responses, and synaptic activity, and many others (Alberti and Hyman, 2021; Strom and Brangwynne, 2019; Wiegand and Hyman, 2020; Zhao and Zhang, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alberti and Hyman, 2021; Strom and Brangwynne, 2019; Wiegand and Hyman, 2020; Zhao and Zhang, 2020.

claim: Many IDRs can drive phase separation in vitro and in vivo.
source: Many IDRs can drive phase separation in vitro and in vivo and make nonspecific, low-affinity, multivalent contacts with RNAs and other proteins that synergize with high-affinity interaction domains to form extended interaction networks (Banani et al., 2017; Peran and Mittag, 2020; Protter et al., 2018; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Peran and Mittag, 2020; Protter et al., 2018; Sanders et al., 2020.

claim: IDRs make nonspecific, low-affinity, multivalent contacts with RNAs and other proteins that synergize with high-affinity interaction domains to form extended interaction networks.
source: Many IDRs can drive phase separation in vitro and in vivo and make nonspecific, low-affinity, multivalent contacts with RNAs and other proteins that synergize with high-affinity interaction domains to form extended interaction networks (Banani et al., 2017; Peran and Mittag, 2020; Protter et al., 2018; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Peran and Mittag, 2020; Protter et al., 2018; Sanders et al., 2020.

claim: Biomolecular condensates are complex coacervates that are governed by principles of polymer physics.
source: These 'biomolecular condensates' are complex coacervates that are governed by principles of polymer physics and can undergo phase transitions between liquid-like, gel-like, and more solid, semi-crystalline states (Brangwynne et al., 2015; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2015 and Shin and Brangwynne, 2017.

claim: Biomolecular condensates can undergo phase transitions between liquid-like, gel-like, and more solid, semi-crystalline states.
source: These 'biomolecular condensates' are complex coacervates that are governed by principles of polymer physics and can undergo phase transitions between liquid-like, gel-like, and more solid, semi-crystalline states (Brangwynne et al., 2015; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2015 and Shin and Brangwynne, 2017.

claim: Hydrogels contain fibrils of stacked beta-sheets that can harden into irreversible amyloids linked to the etiology of various diseases.
source: Whereas condensed liquid droplets undergo rapid local motions, hydrogels contain fibrils of stacked beta-sheets that can harden into irreversible amyloids that are linked to the etiology of various diseases, most notably neurological and age-related pathologies (Alberti and Hyman, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alberti and Hyman, 2021.

claim: In vivo, 'dissolvases' such as protein kinases and ATP-driven RNA helicases are engaged to maintain fluidity of biomolecular condensates.
source: In vivo, 'dissolvases' such as protein kinases and ATP-driven RNA helicases are engaged to maintain fluidity, and these active processes prevent solidification as condensates age (Hubstenberger et al., 2013; Nott et al., 2015; Rai et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hubstenberger et al., 2013; Nott et al., 2015; Rai et al., 2018.

claim: Two previously uncharacterized paralogous proteins, C38D4.4 and F58G11.3, were strongly enriched and highly significant in MEG-3 co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Two previously uncharacterized paralogous proteins, C38D4.4 and F58G11.3, were strongly enriched and highly significant (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: C38D4.4 and F58G11.3 contain extensive serine-rich, disordered regions that comprise 60–65% of their length.
source: Like MEG-3, these proteins contain extensive serine-rich, disordered regions that comprise 60–65% of their length (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A single major isoform for each MIP protein was detected in vivo using 3xFLAG-tagged proteins expressed in mixed-stage animals.
source: A single major isoform for each protein was detected in vivo using 3xFLAG-tagged proteins expressed in mixed-stage animals (Figure 1C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Both C38D4.4 and F58G11.3 interact directly with MEG-3 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: Both proteins interact directly with MEG-3 in yeast two-hybrid assays (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The genes C38D4.4 and F58G11.3 have been named mip-1 and mip-2, respectively.
source: We have named the corresponding genes mip-1 (C38D4.4) and mip-2 (F58G11.3).
evidence: Stated in the text.

claim: MIP-1 and MIP-2 contain two conserved ~100-residue globular LOTUS domains in the N-terminal half of each protein.
source: A combination of primary sequence analysis and predictions of secondary and tertiary structure revealed the presence of two conserved ~100-residue globular LOTUS domains in the N-terminal half of each MIP, separated by a mostly disordered region of ~120–140 residues (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two LOTUS domains in MIP-1 and MIP-2 are separated by a mostly disordered region of ~120–140 residues.
source: A combination of primary sequence analysis and predictions of secondary and tertiary structure revealed the presence of two conserved ~100-residue globular LOTUS domains in the N-terminal half of each MIP, separated by a mostly disordered region of ~120–140 residues (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: LOTUS domains are found in all kingdoms of life and occur in proteins with diverse domain architectures.
source: LOTUS domains are found in all kingdoms of life and occur in proteins with diverse domain architectures (Anantharaman et al., 2010; Callebaut and Mornon, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anantharaman et al., 2010 and Callebaut and Mornon, 2010.

claim: LOTUS domains mediate specific protein-protein interactions and/or bind RNA.
source: Bioinformatic analyses and experimental evidence indicate that LOTUS domains mediate specific protein-protein interactions and/or bind RNA.
evidence: Stated as a general conclusion from bioinformatic and experimental evidence.

claim: Two LOTUS variants have been distinguished: the minimal LOTUS (mLOTUS) and the extended LOTUS (eLOTUS).
source: Two LOTUS variants have been distinguished: the minimal LOTUS (mLOTUS) and the extended LOTUS (eLOTUS), whose defining feature is an additional C-terminal alpha-helix in a region that appears disordered in minimal LOTUS domains (Jeske et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jeske et al., 2017.

claim: The defining feature of eLOTUS is an additional C-terminal alpha-helix in a region that appears disordered in minimal LOTUS domains.
source: Two LOTUS variants have been distinguished: the minimal LOTUS (mLOTUS) and the extended LOTUS (eLOTUS), whose defining feature is an additional C-terminal alpha-helix in a region that appears disordered in minimal LOTUS domains (Jeske et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jeske et al., 2017.

claim: Binding of RNA G-quadruplex secondary structures is an ancient conserved function of mLOTUS domains across kingdoms.
source: A recent study has identified binding of RNA G-quadruplex secondary structures as an ancient conserved function of mLOTUS domains across kingdoms, and suggests that protein binding by eLOTUS domains may be a more recent evolutionary innovation (Ding et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ding et al., 2020.

claim: Protein binding by eLOTUS domains may be a more recent evolutionary innovation.
source: A recent study has identified binding of RNA G-quadruplex secondary structures as an ancient conserved function of mLOTUS domains across kingdoms, and suggests that protein binding by eLOTUS domains may be a more recent evolutionary innovation (Ding et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ding et al., 2020.

claim: Superpositions of LOTUS domain models from worm, fly, and human display clear structural similarity.
source: Superpositions of LOTUS domain models from worm, fly, and human display clear structural similarity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1b,c).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1b,c.

claim: Multiple alignments of LOTUS domains from diverse species show very low sequence identity (10–16%).
source: Although multiple alignments of LOTUS domains from diverse species show very low sequence identity (10–16%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), the ten most conserved residues are predicted to form part of the hydrophobic core and thus would be expected to help stabilize the tertiary structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The ten most conserved residues in LOTUS domains are predicted to form part of the hydrophobic core and help stabilize the tertiary structure.
source: Although multiple alignments of LOTUS domains from diverse species show very low sequence identity (10–16%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), the ten most conserved residues are predicted to form part of the hydrophobic core and thus would be expected to help stabilize the tertiary structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Homology models of all four MIP LOTUS domains contain a clearly identifiable α5 helix.
source: Homology models of all four MIP LOTUS domains contain a clearly identifiable α5 helix (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and can thus be classified as eLOTUS domains like that in the Drosophila germline protein Oskar.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All four MIP LOTUS domains can be classified as eLOTUS domains like that in the Drosophila germline protein Oskar.
source: Homology models of all four MIP LOTUS domains contain a clearly identifiable α5 helix (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and can thus be classified as eLOTUS domains like that in the Drosophila germline protein Oskar.
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All metazoan LOTUS proteins studied so far are critical for normal germ cell development.
source: All metazoan LOTUS proteins studied so far are critical for normal germ cell development.
evidence: Stated as a general conclusion from prior studies.

claim: In Drosophila, Oskar and the Tudor domain proteins Tejas and Tapas recruit Vasa to germ granules in developing egg chambers.
source: In Drosophila, Oskar and the Tudor domain proteins Tejas and Tapas (homologs of mammalian TDRD5 and TDRD7) recruit Vasa to germ granules in developing egg chambers, where they directly bind and stimulate its activity to regulate translation of developmentally important mRNAs or promote piRNA amplification (Jeske et al., 2015; Jeske et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jeske et al., 2015 and Jeske et al., 2017.

claim: Oskar, Tejas, and Tapas directly bind and stimulate Vasa activity to regulate translation of developmentally important mRNAs or promote piRNA amplification in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, Oskar and the Tudor domain proteins Tejas and Tapas (homologs of mammalian TDRD5 and TDRD7) recruit Vasa to germ granules in developing egg chambers, where they directly bind and stimulate its activity to regulate translation of developmentally important mRNAs or promote piRNA amplification (Jeske et al., 2015; Jeske et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jeske et al., 2015 and Jeske et al., 2017.

claim: In the nuage in Drosophila nurse cells, Vasa is essential for the Ping-Pong piRNA amplification system.
source: In the nuage in nurse cells, Vasa is essential for the Ping-Pong piRNA amplification system, where it helps drive the exchange of piRNA intermediates between Argonaute proteins (Xiol et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xiol et al., 2014.

claim: Drosophila MARF1 contains six mLOTUS domains and regulates oocyte maturation by recruiting the CCR4-NOT complex.
source: Drosophila MARF1 contains six mLOTUS domains and regulates oocyte maturation by recruiting the CCR4-NOT complex, which regulates polyadenylation, to inhibit translation of a cyclin mRNA (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2018.

claim: Mouse MARF1 contains eight mLOTUS domains.
source: Mouse MARF1, which contains eight mLOTUS domains, displays mLOTUS-dependent RNA cleavage activity and protects against retrotransposons during oocyte development (Yao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yao et al., 2018.

claim: Mouse MARF1 displays mLOTUS-dependent RNA cleavage activity and protects against retrotransposons during oocyte development.
source: Mouse MARF1, which contains eight mLOTUS domains, displays mLOTUS-dependent RNA cleavage activity and protects against retrotransposons during oocyte development (Yao et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yao et al., 2018.

claim: Single-gene RNAi depletions of mip-1 or mip-2 elicited no evident phenotypes.
source: Single-gene RNAi depletions elicited no evident phenotypes, whereas simultaneous depletion of both mip genes produced sterile animals at 25°C.
evidence: Stated in the text as an experimental result.

claim: Simultaneous depletion of both mip-1 and mip-2 by RNAi produced sterile animals at 25°C.
source: Single-gene RNAi depletions elicited no evident phenotypes, whereas simultaneous depletion of both mip genes produced sterile animals at 25°C.
evidence: Stated in the text as an experimental result.

claim: Continuous RNAi by feeding at 25°C over three generations resulted in progressively smaller brood sizes and embryonic lethality in the progeny of non-sterile worms.
source: Continuous RNAi by feeding at 25°C over three generations resulted in progressively smaller brood sizes and embryonic lethality in the progeny of the non-sterile worms, with the F2 generation showing almost complete sterility (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The F2 generation of mip-1;mip-2 RNAi-treated animals showed almost complete sterility.
source: Continuous RNAi by feeding at 25°C over three generations resulted in progressively smaller brood sizes and embryonic lethality in the progeny of the non-sterile worms, with the F2 generation showing almost complete sterility (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The mip-1Δ;mip-2Δ double null mutant displayed a strong mortal germ line (Mrt) phenotype, resulting in complete sterility after five generations at 20°C.
source: While all three strains appeared superficially wild type (WT), the double null displayed a strong mortal germ line (Mrt) phenotype, resulting in complete sterility after five generations at 20°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Upon shifting to 25°C, sterility in the individual mip-1Δ and mip-2Δ strains increased from ~3% to 10–15% between F1 and F2 generations.
source: Upon shifting to 25°C, all three strains displayed a rapid increase in sterility over just two generations: between F1 and F2 generations, sterility in the individual mip-1Δ and mip-2Δ strains increased from ~3% to 10–15%, and in the mip-1Δ;mip-2Δ from ~50% to 70–80%.
evidence: Stated in the text as an experimental result.

claim: Upon shifting to 25°C, sterility in the mip-1Δ;mip-2Δ double mutant increased from ~50% to 70–80% between F1 and F2 generations.
source: Upon shifting to 25°C, all three strains displayed a rapid increase in sterility over just two generations: between F1 and F2 generations, sterility in the individual mip-1Δ and mip-2Δ strains increased from ~3% to 10–15%, and in the mip-1Δ;mip-2Δ from ~50% to 70–80%.
evidence: Stated in the text as an experimental result.

claim: A diverse range of specific germline phenotypes progressively increased in frequency and severity across several generations in mip-1(RNAi);mip-2(RNAi) treated animals.
source: We observed a diverse range of specific germline phenotypes that progressively increased in frequency and severity across several generations in both mip-1(RNAi);mip-2(RNAi) treated animals (Figure 2B,D) and mip-1Δ;mip-2Δ lines at 25°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Phenotypes in mip-1;mip-2 mutants ranged from minor defects to almost complete lack of detectable germline tissue.
source: Phenotypes ranged from minor defects to almost complete lack of detectable germline tissue and included defects in mitotic proliferation, progression from mitosis to meiosis, pachytene exit, the switch from spermatogenesis to oogenesis, and the formation of normal gametes (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Stated in the text as an experimental observation.

claim: Phenotypes in mip-1;mip-2 mutants included defects in mitotic proliferation, progression from mitosis to meiosis, pachytene exit, the switch from spermatogenesis to oogenesis, and the formation of normal gametes.
source: Phenotypes ranged from minor defects to almost complete lack of detectable germline tissue and included defects in mitotic proliferation, progression from mitosis to meiosis, pachytene exit, the switch from spermatogenesis to oogenesis, and the formation of normal gametes (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Stated in the text as an experimental observation.

claim: A small proportion of mip-1;mip-2 mutant animals displayed a 'Gogo' phenotype (germ line-oocyte-germ line-oocyte).
source: A small proportion of animals displayed an additional 'Gogo' phenotype (germ line-oocyte-germ line-oocyte) (Eberhard et al., 2013; Sendoel et al., 2019), resembling a duplication of the oogenic program (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B, with citations to Eberhard et al., 2013 and Sendoel et al., 2019.

claim: The spectrum of phenotypes in mip-1;mip-2 mutants suggests that developmental switches regulating cell state transitions become compromised in germ lines where MIPs function is strongly reduced or abrogated.
source: This spectrum of phenotypes suggests that developmental switches regulating cell state transitions become compromised in germ lines where MIPs function is strongly reduced or abrogated.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the observed phenotypes.

claim: The most extreme germline phenotype in mip-1;mip-2 mutants consisted of only a few germ cells in close proximity to the DTC.
source: The most extreme germline phenotype consisted of only a few germ cells in close proximity to the DTC (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The diameters of the remaining germ cell nuclei in the most extreme mip-1;mip-2 phenotype measured around 1.8 times larger than those in the distal proliferative zone of control germ lines.
source: The diameters of the remaining germ cell nuclei measured around 1.8 times larger than those in the distal proliferative zone of control germ lines (Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The unusual appearance and small number of remaining nuclei in the most extreme mip-1;mip-2 phenotype suggest that they have lost their capacity for self-renewal.
source: The unusual appearance and small number of remaining nuclei suggest that they have lost their capacity for self-renewal, and we infer that such germ lines have exhausted their pool of stem cells.
evidence: Stated as an inference from the observed phenotype.

claim: MIP-1 is omnipresent throughout development, localizing exclusively to the germline precursor lineage (from P0 through P4) and remaining prominent in the germline progenitor cells Z2 and Z3.

claim: The Mrt phenotype commonly occurs in association with defects in heritable RNAi and transgenerational epigenetic inheritance (TEI).
source: The Mrt phenotype (Ahmed and Hodgkin, 2000) commonly occurs in association with defects in heritable RNAi and transgenerational epigenetic inheritance (TEI), which arise through misregulation of small RNA pathways (Simon et al., 2014; Spracklin et al., 2017) and downstream chromatin modifications (Smelick and Ahmed, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ahmed and Hodgkin, 2000; Simon et al., 2014; Spracklin et al., 2017; Smelick and Ahmed, 2005.

claim: P granules are the primary site of piRNA and siRNA biogenesis in the C. elegans germ line.
source: P granules are the primary site of piRNA and siRNA biogenesis in the C. elegans germ line, and several recent studies have described a role for them in balancing small RNA pathways (Dodson and Kennedy, 2019; Lev et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dodson and Kennedy, 2019; Lev et al., 2019; Ouyang et al., 2019.

claim: Stoichiometry of Argonautes and other small RNA pathway components is important for transgenerational memory and for tuning the levels of developmentally important transcripts.
source: Since different factors compete for some of the same machinery, stoichiometry of Argonautes and other small RNA pathway components is important not only for transgenerational memory, but also to tune the levels of developmentally important transcripts (Dodson and Kennedy, 2019; Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2016; Seth et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dodson and Kennedy, 2019; Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2016; Seth et al., 2018.

claim: Vasa helicases are essential for both mRNA regulation and small RNA processing in the germ line of many species.
source: Vasa helicases are essential for both mRNA regulation and small RNA processing in the germ line of many species (Lasko, 2013; Voronina et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lasko, 2013 and Voronina et al., 2011.

claim: In both worms and flies, Vasa homologs associate with Argonautes and play a role in piRNA biogenesis and siRNA amplification.
source: In both worms and flies, Vasa homologs associate with Argonautes and play a role in piRNA biogenesis and siRNA amplification (Marnik et al., 2019; Xiol et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marnik et al., 2019 and Xiol et al., 2014.

claim: In C. elegans, GLH-1 interacts with miRISC complexes within P granules to regulate translation and storage of target transcripts.
source: In C. elegans, GLH-1 also interacts with miRISC complexes within P granules to regulate translation and storage of target transcripts (Dallaire et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dallaire et al., 2018.

claim: Regulation of RNA helicase activity can either lock RNP complexes or remodel them by promoting RNA transfer between complexes, release, and turnover.
source: Regulation of RNA helicase activity can either lock RNP complexes or remodel them by promoting RNA transfer between complexes, release, and turnover – all of which influence the composition, organization, and biophysical properties of condensates (Marnik et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marnik et al., 2019.

claim: The dissolution of P granules upon loss of MIPs function is expected to have broad-ranging consequences on RNA metabolism.
source: Thus, the dissolution of P granules upon loss of MIPs function is expected to have broad-ranging consequences on RNA metabolism.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an inference from the role of MIPs.

claim: Spatiotemporal protein expression in the C. elegans germ line is primarily driven by post-transcriptional regulation.
source: Spatiotemporal protein expression in the C. elegans germ line is primarily driven by post-transcriptional regulation (Merritt et al., 2008), and P granules positioned over nuclear pores facilitate this by surveilling mRNAs as they exit germline nuclei (Sheth et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Merritt et al., 2008 and Sheth et al., 2010.

claim: P granules positioned over nuclear pores facilitate post-transcriptional regulation by surveilling mRNAs as they exit germline nuclei.
source: Spatiotemporal protein expression in the C. elegans germ line is primarily driven by post-transcriptional regulation (Merritt et al., 2008), and P granules positioned over nuclear pores facilitate this by surveilling mRNAs as they exit germline nuclei (Sheth et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheth et al., 2010.

claim: The highly pleiotropic phenotypes in mip-1;mip-2 mutants likely reflect disruption of key post-transcriptional regulatory events.
source: Given that P granules are severely compromised in mip-1;mip-2 mutants, their highly pleiotropic phenotypes likely reflect disruption of key post-transcriptional regulatory events.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an inference from the role of P granules.

claim: The Gogo phenotype has been linked to alterations in the Ras/MAPK pathway.
source: While the proximal cause in mip mutants remains to be determined, the Gogo phenotype has been linked to alterations in the Ras/MAPK pathway, which directs developmental transitions in the germ line and is involved in regulating both physiological and DNA-damage-induced apoptosis (Eberhard et al., 2013; Sendoel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eberhard et al., 2013 and Sendoel et al., 2019.

claim: The broad range of mip-1;mip-2 phenotypes suggests that cells in the germ line cannot properly maintain their state or manage state transitions upon prolonged absence of MIPs function.
source: The broad range of mip-1;mip-2 phenotypes we see suggests that cells in the germ line cannot properly maintain their state or manage state transitions upon prolonged absence of MIPs function.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the phenotypes.

claim: MEG-3 nonspecifically recruits numerous mRNAs into P granules in vivo.
source: MEG-3 nonspecifically recruits numerous mRNAs into P granules in vivo (Lee et al., 2020), and in vitro it forms molecular condensates with RNA, which lowers its saturation concentration (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2020.

claim: In vitro, MEG-3 forms molecular condensates with RNA, which lowers its saturation concentration.
source: MEG-3 nonspecifically recruits numerous mRNAs into P granules in vivo (Lee et al., 2020), and in vitro it forms molecular condensates with RNA, which lowers its saturation concentration (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Putnam et al., 2019.

claim: Antagonistic regulation of MEG-3 by PP2A phosphatase and MBK-2 kinase, and competition for RNA with anteriorly localized MEX-5, create a permissive environment for P granule assembly only in the posterior of the zygote.
source: Antagonistic regulation of MEG-3 by PP2A phosphatase and MBK-2 kinase, a master regulator of the oocyte-to-embryo transition, and competition for RNA with anteriorly localized MEX-5, create a permissive environment for P granule assembly only in the posterior of the zygote (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2009 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: The MIPs and MEG-3 have a synergistic relationship in P granule formation in the early embryo.
source: The MIPs and MEG-3 have a synergistic relationship in P granule formation in the early embryo: when either MEG-3 or mip-1/mip-2 are absent, other P granule components are mostly diffuse in the zygote.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The MIPs appear to work together with MEG-3 to decrease the critical concentration for P granule condensation.
source: Therefore, the MIPs appear to work together with MEG-3 to decrease the critical concentration for P granule condensation.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: PGL-3 was significantly more mobile than MEG-3, MIP-1, MIP-2, and GLH-1 in two-cell embryos.
source: We found that PGL-3 was significantly more mobile than MEG-3, MIP-1, MIP-2, and GLH-1 in two-cell embryos, and that between the 2- and 12-cell stage its diffusivity slowed to match that of the other four proteins.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Between the 2- and 12-cell stage, PGL-3 diffusivity slowed to match that of MEG-3, MIP-1, MIP-2, and GLH-1.
source: We found that PGL-3 was significantly more mobile than MEG-3, MIP-1, MIP-2, and GLH-1 in two-cell embryos, and that between the 2- and 12-cell stage its diffusivity slowed to match that of the other four proteins.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: PGL-3 becomes more firmly tethered within P granules in conjunction with their transition from free-floating to perinuclear structures.
source: PGL-3 therefore seems to become more firmly tethered within P granules in conjunction with their transition from free-floating to perinuclear structures, leading us to conclude that the biophysical properties of P granules in the embryo evolve over time.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The biophysical properties of P granules in the embryo evolve over time.
source: PGL-3 therefore seems to become more firmly tethered within P granules in conjunction with their transition from free-floating to perinuclear structures, leading us to conclude that the biophysical properties of P granules in the embryo evolve over time.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: MEG-3 has been described to form a ribbon-like structure surrounding and penetrating PGL granules in vivo.
source: MEG-3 has been described to form a ribbon-like structure surrounding and penetrating PGL granules in vivo (Wang et al., 2014) and to form an outer layer encasing a mobile PGL phase in reconstituted assemblies in vitro (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014.

claim: MEG-3 has been described to form an outer layer encasing a mobile PGL phase in reconstituted assemblies in vitro.
source: MEG-3 has been described to form a ribbon-like structure surrounding and penetrating PGL granules in vivo (Wang et al., 2014) and to form an outer layer encasing a mobile PGL phase in reconstituted assemblies in vitro (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Putnam et al., 2019.

claim: As visualized by super-resolution imaging, MEG-3 appears to permeate the full volume of cytoplasmic P granules and is fully interspersed with MIP-2 at least through the eight-cell stage.
source: As visualized here by super-resolution imaging, MEG-3 appears to permeate the full volume of cytoplasmic P granules and is fully interspersed with MIP-2 at least through the eight-cell stage, suggesting that the higher mobility of PGL-3 in very early embryos occurs in the absence of spatially distinct, immiscible phases.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The higher mobility of PGL-3 in very early embryos occurs in the absence of spatially distinct, immiscible phases.
source: As visualized here by super-resolution imaging, MEG-3 appears to permeate the full volume of cytoplasmic P granules and is fully interspersed with MIP-2 at least through the eight-cell stage, suggesting that the higher mobility of PGL-3 in very early embryos occurs in the absence of spatially distinct, immiscible phases.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the imaging data.

claim: The MIPs play a central role in maintaining P granule integrity at all developmental stages.
source: The MIPs play a central role in maintaining P granule integrity at all developmental stages.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Embryos depleted of meg-3 do eventually form P granules, since meg-3 mutant larvae and adults show normal expression and localization of the MIPs and other P granule proteins in the germ line.
source: In contrast, embryos depleted of meg-3 do eventually form P granules, since meg-3 mutant larvae and adults show normal expression and localization of the MIPs and other P granule proteins in the germ line.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: At least two distinct mechanisms exist to drive P granule assembly in vivo: nucleation and growth in the early embryo that depends on both MEG-3 and MIPs; and a MIP-dependent, MEG-3-independent process that nucleates and maintains P granules at the nuclear periphery later in germline development.
source: Therefore, at least two distinct mechanisms exist to drive P granule assembly in vivo: nucleation and growth in the early embryo that depends on both MEG-3 and MIPs; and a MIP-dependent, MEG-3-independent process that nucleates and maintains P granules at the nuclear periphery later in germline development.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Phase separation of P granule components in the early embryo is not strictly required when other developmental determinants such as MEX-5 remain asymmetrically distributed in the zygote.
source: This is consistent with the finding that phase separation of P granule components in the early embryo is not strictly required when other developmental determinants such as MEX-5 remain asymmetrically distributed in the zygote (Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallo et al., 2010.

claim: In WT embryos, P granules begin attaching to the nuclear periphery in the P2 cell, when the P lineage is thought to be transcriptionally silent.
source: In WT embryos, P granules begin attaching to the nuclear periphery in the P2 cell, when the P lineage is thought to be transcriptionally silent, and form caps over nuclear pores throughout the rest of germline development (Pitt et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pitt et al., 2000.

claim: P granules form caps over nuclear pores throughout the rest of germline development.
source: In WT embryos, P granules begin attaching to the nuclear periphery in the P2 cell, when the P lineage is thought to be transcriptionally silent, and form caps over nuclear pores throughout the rest of germline development (Pitt et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pitt et al., 2000.

claim: In the adult germ line, perinuclear granules assemble around RNA as it exits the nucleus.
source: In the adult germ line, perinuclear granules assemble around RNA as it exits the nucleus, and transcription and mRNA export are required for their proper morphology (Sheth et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheth et al., 2010.

claim: Transcription and mRNA export are required for proper morphology of perinuclear granules in the adult germ line.
source: In the adult germ line, perinuclear granules assemble around RNA as it exits the nucleus, and transcription and mRNA export are required for their proper morphology (Sheth et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheth et al., 2010.

claim: Association with membranes can reduce the saturation concentration for condensation by localized recruitment of components and restricting diffusion.
source: Association with membranes can reduce the saturation concentration for condensation by localized recruitment of components and restricting diffusion (Snead and Gladfelter, 2019; Söding et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Snead and Gladfelter, 2019 and Söding et al., 2020.

claim: The perinuclear localization of MIP-1 and MIP-2 in the germ line, independent of other P granule components, raises the possibility that they nucleate the formation of P granules at the nuclear periphery.
source: The perinuclear localization of MIP-1 and MIP-2 in the germ line, independent of other P granule components, raises the possibility that they nucleate the formation of P granules at the nuclear periphery.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a speculation based on the data.

claim: P granules likely attach directly to nuclear pore complexes (NPCs).
source: P granules likely attach directly to nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), as knockdown of some nuclear pore proteins causes them to detach (Updike and Strome, 2009; Voronina and Seydoux, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Updike and Strome, 2009 and Voronina and Seydoux, 2010.

claim: MIP-1 is an obvious candidate for tethering granules to NPCs.
source: Since MIP-1 typically appears closer to the base of perinuclear P granules than MIP-2 and is required for perinuclear localization of P granules, it is an obvious candidate for tethering granules to NPCs.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an inference from the localization data.

claim: The MIPs may work together with GLH-1 to maintain perinuclear association of P granules.
source: The MIPs may work together with GLH-1 to maintain perinuclear association, since the FG repeats of GLH-1 are also necessary (but not sufficient) for its perinuclear localization in the embryo or when expressed ectopically (Marnik et al., 2019; Updike et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a speculation, supported by citations to Marnik et al., 2019 and Updike et al., 2011.

claim: The FG repeats of GLH-1 are necessary (but not sufficient) for its perinuclear localization in the embryo or when expressed ectopically.
source: The MIPs may work together with GLH-1 to maintain perinuclear association, since the FG repeats of GLH-1 are also necessary (but not sufficient) for its perinuclear localization in the embryo or when expressed ectopically (Marnik et al., 2019; Updike et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marnik et al., 2019 and Updike et al., 2011.

claim: The FG repeats of GLH-1 are thought to help tether GLH-1 to nuclear pores through hydrophobic interactions with FG repeat proteins in the NPC matrix.
source: The FG repeats are thought to help tether GLH-1 to nuclear pores through hydrophobic interactions with FG repeat proteins in the NPC matrix.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of prior findings.

claim: GLH-1 and PGL-1 readily diffuse upon treatment with 1,6-hexanediol.
source: In support of this idea, GLH-1 and PGL-1 readily diffuse upon treatment with 1,6-hexanediol (Updike et al., 2011 and this study).
evidence: Supported by citation to Updike et al., 2011 and data from this study.

claim: The MIPs are partially resistant to hexanediol treatment and therefore must employ additional interaction forces to engage other P granule and/or nuclear pore components.
source: In contrast, The MIPs are partially resistant to this treatment and therefore must employ additional interaction forces to engage other P granule and/or nuclear pore components.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an inference from the hexanediol treatment data.

claim: GLH-1 depends on MIP-1 in addition to its FG repeats to help anchor it within P granules.
source: GLH-1 also depends on MIP-1 in addition to its FG repeats to help anchor it within P granules, since its mobility increases when MIP-1 is depleted.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the FRAP data.

claim: P granules and other biomolecular condensates are dynamic, non-equilibrium structures whose nucleation and growth are driven by a combination of high-affinity protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions and weak multivalent interactions between IDRs and with RNAs.
source: P granules and other biomolecular condensates are dynamic, non-equilibrium structures whose nucleation and growth are driven by a combination of high-affinity protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions and weak multivalent interactions between IDRs and with RNAs (Banani et al., 2017; Hyman et al., 2014; Mittag and Parker, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Hyman et al., 2014; Mittag and Parker, 2018.

claim: The biophysical properties of biomolecular condensates are underpinned by a variety of molecular forces, including charge-charge, dipole-dipole, cation-pi, and pi-pi stacking interactions.
source: Their biophysical properties are underpinned by a variety of molecular forces, including charge-charge, dipole-dipole, cation-pi, and pi-pi stacking interactions (Brangwynne et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brangwynne et al., 2015.

claim: The biophysical properties of biomolecular condensates are influenced by solvent properties like pH and ionic strength, environmental factors such as temperature, and by the concentration, composition, and stoichiometry of their components.
source: These interactions are influenced by solvent properties like pH and ionic strength, environmental factors such as temperature, and by the concentration, composition, and stoichiometry of their components.
evidence: Stated as general knowledge about biomolecular condensates.

claim: In vivo, the formation and organization of biomolecular condensates are regulated by cellular and developmental cues.
source: In vivo, the formation and organization of biomolecular condensates are regulated by cellular and developmental cues (Söding et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Söding et al., 2020.

claim: High concentrations of free RNA and translational repressors tend to promote phase separation.
source: High concentrations of free RNA and translational repressors tend to promote phase separation (Langdon and Gladfelter, 2018), whereas a wide variety of post-translational modifications (PTMs) – including Arg/Lys methylation, Lys acetylation, Arg citrullination, Ser/Thr and Tyr phosphorylation, Ser/Thr glycosylation, and SUMOylation – can either promote or antagonize LLPS by altering electrostatics and binding valency (Brangwynne et al., 2015; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Snead and Gladfelter, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Langdon and Gladfelter, 2018.

claim: A wide variety of post-translational modifications can either promote or antagonize LLPS by altering electrostatics and binding valency.
source: High concentrations of free RNA and translational repressors tend to promote phase separation (Langdon and Gladfelter, 2018), whereas a wide variety of post-translational modifications (PTMs) – including Arg/Lys methylation, Lys acetylation, Arg citrullination, Ser/Thr and Tyr phosphorylation, Ser/Thr glycosylation, and SUMOylation – can either promote or antagonize LLPS by altering electrostatics and binding valency (Brangwynne et al., 2015; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Snead and Gladfelter, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brangwynne et al., 2015; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Snead and Gladfelter, 2019.

claim: PTMs provide a mechanism for rapid and reversible control of material properties that allow tunable dynamic responses to changing conditions in biomolecular condensates.
source: By changing the nature and strength of molecular interactions, PTMs thus provide a mechanism for rapid and reversible control of material properties that allow tunable dynamic responses to changing conditions.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the role of PTMs.

claim: RNA helicases play active roles in remodeling biomolecular condensates by regulating RNP dynamics.
source: RNA helicases also play active roles in remodeling biomolecular condensates by regulating RNP dynamics (Linder and Jankowsky, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Linder and Jankowsky, 2011.

claim: ATP-binding promotes condensation, and ATPase-coupled RNA duplex unwinding and release of ssRNA promote fluidity and RNA flux through phase-separated compartments.
source: ATP-binding promotes condensation, and ATPase-coupled RNA duplex unwinding and release of ssRNA promote fluidity and RNA flux through phase-separated compartments (Hondele et al., 2019; Hubstenberger et al., 2013; Marnik et al., 2019; Nott et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hondele et al., 2019; Hubstenberger et al., 2013; Marnik et al., 2019; Nott et al., 2015.

claim: ATP-dependent Vasa helicases have long been associated with essential functions in the germ line, where they engage a variety of RNP complexes involved in translational regulation and small RNA biogenesis.
source: ATP-dependent Vasa helicases have long been associated with essential functions in the germ line, where they engage a variety of RNP complexes involved in translational regulation and small RNA biogenesis (Dallaire et al., 2018; Lasko, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dallaire et al., 2018 and Lasko, 2013.

claim: Vasa helicases such as GLH-1 play a central role in coordinating numerous dynamic RNA regulatory processes within germ granules.
source: Vasa helicases such as GLH-1 therefore play a central role in coordinating numerous dynamic RNA regulatory processes within germ granules, where their activity would be expected to tune both biophysical properties and information flow.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the role of Vasa helicases.

claim: Many of the defects elicited in the absence of MIPs function could reflect a failure to properly organize different types of RNP reaction centers that require RNA helicase activity within P granules.
source: Since the MIPs directly bind and recruit the C. elegans Vasa homolog GLH-1 to P granules, many of the defects elicited in the absence of MIPs function could reflect a failure to properly organize different types of RNP reaction centers that require RNA helicase activity within them.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a speculation based on the data.

claim: Biomolecular condensates enhance the robustness of switch-like cellular decisions and can also act as rheostats to tune outputs.
source: The broad spectrum of germline phenotypes we observe may be viewed in light of recent findings that biomolecular condensates enhance the robustness of switch-like cellular decisions and can also act as rheostats to tune outputs (Klosin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klosin et al., 2020.

claim: Phase separation selectively increases the efficiency of molecular reactions, both by concentrating specific molecular machinery and by excluding antagonistic regulators.
source: This is because phase separation selectively increases the efficiency of molecular reactions, both by concentrating specific molecular machinery and by excluding antagonistic regulators (Snead and Gladfelter, 2019; Söding et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Snead and Gladfelter, 2019 and Söding et al., 2020.

claim: P granules provide a protected compartment for mRNA surveillance by small RNA pathways and translational regulators.
source: P granules provide a protected compartment for mRNA surveillance by small RNA pathways and translational regulators.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary of P granule function.

claim: Storage and regulation of transcripts encoding developmental determinants are promoted by a combination of mRNA stabilization and translational repression, as well as exclusion of assembled ribosomes.
source: Storage and regulation of transcripts encoding developmental determinants are promoted by a combination of mRNA stabilization and translational repression, as well as exclusion of assembled ribosomes (Lee et al., 2020; Marnik et al., 2019; Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2020; Marnik et al., 2019; Parker et al., 2020.

claim: Phase separation generates a sequestered environment that helps buffer regulatory processes that contribute to the proper timing and execution of developmental transitions.
source: Thus, while phase separation may not be absolutely required for the activity of individual P granule components, it generates a sequestered environment that helps buffer regulatory processes that contribute to the proper timing and execution of developmental transitions.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the role of phase separation.

claim: The gradual appearance of wide-ranging developmental defects and consequent loss of reproductive potential in the absence of key germ granule components are consistent with the current view of how molecular condensates contribute to cellular robustness.
source: The gradual appearance of wide-ranging developmental defects and consequent loss of reproductive potential in the absence of key germ granule components are therefore entirely consistent with the current view of how molecular condensates contribute to cellular robustness.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: The identification of LOTUS-domain proteins that may organize and scaffold various RNP assemblies by recruiting a core Vasa helicase is a step forward toward understanding deeply conserved architectural principles of germ granules.
source: The identification of LOTUS-domain proteins that may organize and scaffold various RNP assemblies by recruiting a core Vasa helicase is a step forward toward understanding deeply conserved architectural principles of germ granules.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion as a summary of the significance of the findings.
